item.title: Seasonal icings reveal subsurface water drainage of a Greenland Ice Sheet outlet glacier
item.dc:creator: Rebecca McCerery, Joseph A. Graly, Christopher L. Hansen, Kate Winter, William P. Gilhooly III, Trinity L. Hamilton, … (+13)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, subglacial, glacier, Greenland, outlet glacier, ice core
Ice cores from Isunnguata Sermia’s forefield reveal how proglacial naled and accreted ices form in Greenland. Naledi build up in winter from precipitation and mineral-rich subglacial water, while accreted ice forms in summer through supercooled water upwelling. Geophysical surveys indicate both are fed by subsurface flows potentially originating from the glacier bed. Here, we present the first conceptual model of these formations in Greenland.

item.title: Imaging the Ross Ice Streams of West Antarctica using active source seismology
item.dc:creator: Huw Joseph Horgan, Andrew Robert Gorman, J. Paul Winberry, Sridhar Anandakrishnan, Howard Conway, Gavin B. Dunbar, … (+5)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: ice sheet, ice stream, subglacial, Antarctica
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Knowledge of the past and future of Earth's ice sheets requires us to image beneath the ice surface and into the ice, water, sediment, and rock that lies beneath. An effective way of doing this uses active source seismology. Here we present active source seismic data imaging a diverse range of subglacial environments including subglacial lakes, sub-ice ocean cavities, and geological archives preserving the history of the ice sheets.

item.title: A Basin‐Wise GLOF Susceptibility Assessment in the Western Himalayas: Integrating Remote Sensing‐ GIS and Multi‐Criteria Decision Analysis
item.dc:creator: Rayees Ahmed, Anil Vishnupant Kulkarni
item.description:
Transactions in GIS — matched: glacier, permafrost, remote sensing, climate change
ABSTRACT Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) pose an increasing threat to high mountain environments across the world, especially in the Himalayas where climate change is accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost degradation. This study presents a detailed GLOF susceptibility analysis of the western Himalayas covering five major river basins, ie Satluj, Chenab, Jhelum, Beas, and Ravi by integrating high‐resolution remote sensing data with a multi‐criteria decision‐making approach. A detailed inventory of 1573 glacial lakes was developed using manual delineation of Sentinel‐2A and LISS‐IV images. Forty‐eight potentially dangerous lakes were identified based on size and dam composition. Following the guidelines of NDMA and GAPHAZ, 12 important physical and geomorphic parameters were selected and evaluated using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with the addition of Cumulative Weightage Technique (CWT). AHP Analysis indicated that 20 lakes were high hazard, 23 lakes were medium hazard, and five lakes were low hazard. The basin‐wise analysis revealed that Satluj and Chenab are particularly vulnerable owing to the presence of large and fast‐growing lakes. A temporal assessment of 48 selected potentially dangerous lakes from 2000 to 2024 revealed a 115% increase in total lake area, highlighting their rapid expansion under a warming climate. The susceptibility framework was validated using seven historical GLOF events, all of which had hazard scores > 0.7, in agreement with the high susceptibility lakes identified in this study. The study recommends that detailed field investigations be carried out on high‐hazard lakes including bathymetric surveys, assessments of moraine stability, and real‐time monitoring to validate remote sensing findings and to inform early warning systems. This approach offers a transferable and policy‐relevant framework to support GLOF risk mitigation and climate adaptation planning in glacierized regions. This study relies primarily on remote sensing data, and uncertainties in lake identification and the lack of field validation may affect susceptibility classification.

item.title: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
item.dc:creator: Gökhan Sarigil, Mattia Neri, Francesco Avanzi, Elena Toth
item.description:
Hydrology and earth system sciences — matched: parameterization, downscaling
Abstract. Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a critical hydrological variable for water resource management in mountainous regions, where seasonal snowpacks function as natural reservoirs regulating streamflow and water supply. While high-resolution, observation-constrained regional or national snow products provide reliable daily SWE estimates at fine spatial resolution (less than 1 km), their limited temporal coverage often restricts their use for long-term hydro-climatological studies. Large-scale land-surface products, in which SWE is derived from land-surface model simulations driven by atmospheric reanalyses or regional dynamical downscaling systems, provide multi-decadal coverage, but their reliability may be affected by biases in meteorological forcing, limited topographic representation, and simplified snow process parameterisation, requiring rigorous regional evaluation. This study evaluates the SWE estimates of three large-scale land-surface products, i.e., the global ERA5-Land, the European CERRA-Land, and the Italian VHR-REA_IT, against the national reference dataset IT-SNOW across Italy. The analysis combines grid-scale bias assessment of mean annual SWE and snow cover duration with temporal correlation analysis of daily SWE series, and is complemented by an evaluation of precipitation and temperature biases in each product, providing insight into how each product represents the atmospheric conditions governing snow accumulation and ablation and thereby supporting the interpretation of the identified SWE discrepancies. The results show clear regional differences in product performance, with no single product performing best across all metrics. ERA5-Land shows the strongest temporal correlation with IT-SNOW, but tends to overestimate mean annual SWE and snow cover duration in the Alps. CERRA-Land shows more moderate biases than ERA5-Land in the Italian Alps, but generally underestimates mean annual SWE across most subregions, where autumn and winter precipitation deficits in the forcing limit snow accumulation. Across the Apennines, both ERA5-Land and CERRA-Land tend to underestimate SWE and snow cover duration, particularly in the northern sectors. VHR-REA_IT shows widespread underestimation and the weakest temporal correspondence with IT-SNOW: this may be due to its fully coupled atmosphere–land architecture with no assimilation of meteorological observations. Overall, the results suggest that forcing biases explain a substantial part of the observed SWE discrepancies, although not all of them. This study provides useful insights for the use of SWE estimates from large-scale land-surface products in long-term hydro-climatological assessments over Italy and helps to understand whether the products can be used to evaluate snow dynamics in mountainous regions lacking high-quality benchmark estimates.

item.title: Decadal strengthening of the preceding-winter ENSO influence on subsequent pre-flood-season precipitation over southern China. Part II: Strengthened La Niña teleconnection due to slower decay and enhanced WES feedback
item.dc:creator: Yuqing Li, Lin Chen
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, CMIP
Abstract In Part I, we documented a marked mid-1990s strengthening of the ENSO influence on pre-flood-season (PFS; April–June) rainfall over southern China (SC) and identified the dominant mechanism for the strengthened El Niño teleconnection. Here we focus on La Niña and examine why its influence on SC PFS rainfall strengthens after the mid-1990s. Observations show that La Niña events during 1996–2021 (P2) exhibit a slower decay than those during 1959–1995 (P1), allowing cold sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies to persist into AMJ over the Niño4 region and more strongly suppressing central-Pacific convection. The resulting Matsuno–Gill response induces more pronounced low-level wind anomalies over the western North Pacific (WNP). Together with intensified wind–evaporation–SST (WES) coupling in P2, these wind anomalies more effectively modulate surface latent heat fluxes and amplify local SST and convection anomalies over the WNP, exciting a stronger cyclonic circulation spanning the South China Sea and WNP. The associated northeasterly anomalies enhance cold–dry advection over SC, favoring anomalous subsidence and reduced moisture supply and thereby intensifying SC rainfall deficits during La Niña decay years in P2. CMIP6 historical simulations provide complementary support: models with a stronger WES coupling show a stronger La Niña–SC PFS linkage. These results show that the strengthened La Niña teleconnection arises from the combined effects of slower La Niña decay and enhanced WES coupling, providing a phase-dependent counterpart to the El Niño mechanism identified in Part I and highlighting the importance of accurately representing ENSO evolution and WNP air–sea coupling in seasonal prediction of SC PFS rainfall.

item.title: Leveraging leaf-level optimality processes with explicit acclimation improves global GPP representation in an individual-based DGVM (LPJ-GUESS v4.1.1)
item.dc:creator: Matthew Forrest, Mateus Dantas de Paula, Filipe Gomes de Almeida, Sandy P. Harrison, I. Colin Prentice, Thomas Hickler
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Earth system, climate change
Global photosynthesis on land is a large flow of carbon in the Earth system which underpins food production and ecosystems. It is particularly important to know how it responds to climate change, but current vegetation models do not agree on this. We implemented a new photosynthesis model based on recent theoretical advances into a vegetation model. We found that it improved the representation of photosynthesis when compared both to global data from satellites and detailed site measurements.
